title: Is the AI Apocalypse for Real?
author: Ken Klippenstein
content:

In the debate about what threats artificial intelligence poses, everyone is
trying to sell you something. If you follow the corporate press, artificial
intelligence is a looming mass extinction event waiting to happen. If you
listen to Trump, it's part of the next Cold War with China, meaning we can't
afford to slow down.

For the [appistocracy](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/the-appistocracy-
inaugurates-trump), there's profit in all of the attention -- literally. We
have a new generation of technologists who generate publicity warning of
everything from bioterrorism to the machines taking over. Thus AI is turned
into a "national security" issue; and as such, it is elevated to the same
status as nuclear weapons, deemed too important for interference from a
meddlesome public.

The reality though? Listen to the spy agencies. Though they're far from immune
to threat inflation, these agencies echo none of the hysterics dominating the
news. As the U.S. intelligence community sees it, AI simply magnifies threats
that are already there. And that's basically right. (More on this in a
moment.)

We've all seen the sensational headlines. And it's not just the old school
media. Social media influencers credulously amplify this coverage to their
millions of followers, going viral with talk of human extinction. Thus dire
warnings about a looming AI apocalypse (called things like catastrophic risk,
existential risk or X-risk) dominate Americans' collective imagination.

Then there are the anti-doomers, who run a racket of their own. The most
prominent are Yann LeCun, until the end of last year Meta's chief AI
scientist, and Andrew Ng, who co-founded Google Brain and now runs the venture
studio AI Fund.

In October 2023, LeCun accused Sam Altman, Demis Hassabis and Dario Amodei --
the heads of OpenAI (ChatGPT's developer), Google DeepMind (Gemini) and
Anthropic (Claude) -- of "massive corporate lobbying" aimed at regulatory
capture, warning that if their fearmongering succeeded, a small number of
companies would end up controlling AI. Ng, in an interview the same week,
called the idea that AI could drive humans to extinction a "massively,
colossally dumb idea," and said large tech companies were manufacturing
extinction fear because they would rather not compete with open source.

They may well be right about the motives of the companies they're criticizing;
but they have conflicts of their own.

LeCun and Ng are two of the most high-profile advocates of what's called
"open-weight" AI -- meaning AI whose code is made publicly available in order
to facilitate adoption. Anthropic and OpenAI, by contrast, opted for
proprietary code that they rent to users. The latter would likely benefit from
federal licensing requirements that only the big proprietary players could
afford to comply with, whereas the open-weight businesses would be harmed by
it.

What every faction has in common --from the proponents of some AI apocalypse
to the anti-regulation types -- is their disinterest in responding to the
realistic risks AI poses.

The U.S. intelligence community provides the most reasonable account of the
actual dangers. The Annual Threat Assessment is the U.S. intelligence
community's official list of national security threats: covering things like
China's military, Russian influence operations, drug cartels, etc.

In this year's
[report](https://archive.dni.gov/files/ODNI/documents/assessments/ATA-2026-Unclassified-
Report.pdf), artificial intelligence is described as a threat in three
different ways:

  1. "[I]t is essential to make sure that humans maintain control of the machines and how AI is used."

  2. "These applications, however, also carry risks that require careful human engineering to appropriately mitigate risk of AI autonomy before they are broadly deployed."

  3. "[E]merging technologies such as AI and quantum computing are expected to have a significant impact on national security."

That's the sum total of what the eighteen agencies of the U.S. intelligence
community have to say about the dangers of AI. No human extinction, no
superintelligence, no machine uprising.

As the most recent Department of Homeland Security Threat Assessment [puts
it](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2024-10/24_0930_ia_24-320-ia-
publication-2025-hta-final-30sep24-508.pdf) AI is merely "adding layers of
complexity to the threats we face." It identifies the following five problems:

  * Disinformation, deepfakes, and election interference,

  * Cyber operations and financial crime,

  * Violent extremist exploitation and radicalization,

  * Proliferation of chemical and biological knowledge, and

  * Breaking AI's safety controls, and poisoning the data it trains on.

Virtually all of these threats existed before AI. For instance, AI-fueled
disinformation is the same old propaganda but in greater quantity and speed.
Same with cyber operations and financial crimes (plus maybe some stealth
benefits). As for "extremists" radicalizing people, anyone who's used social
media for the past decade or two knows that is nothing new, either. The
chemical and biological concern goes back to at least the Clinton
administration, biotechnology being the last apocalyptic threat. And the fifth
pertains to situations in which humans have tampered with AI's safety
controls.

I'm not saying any of this isn't worthy of concern. Just that it's not the end
of the world.

The RAND Corporation's _[Global Catastrophic Risk
Assessment](https://www.fie.undef.edu.ar/ceptm/wp-
content/uploads/2024/11/RAND_RRA2981-1.pdf) _analyzed civilizational threats
and concluded that AI is merely an "entropy" engine.

"One can think of AI as adding entropy and chaos to already-wicked problems
that humans face," the RAND report says. "Chaos does not require the
development of superintelligent or supercapable AI and is possible with
existing and near-future AI capabilities."

RAND, I'll remind anyone not familiar, is no dovish institution. The Pentagon-
funded think tank was built to think about thermonuclear war and is hardly shy
about civilizational threats.

RAND's companion
[study](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3034-1.html), _On the
Extinction Risk from Artificial Intelligence_ , explored similar questions
specific to AI. The study identifies three plausible paths to human
extinction, including engineered pathogens, geo-engineering, and nuclear war.

But there are major constraints preventing AI from precipitating any of these
three events, both physical and operational.

RAND expanded on these constraints in a subsequent
[report](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2977-2.html) exploring
whether large language could make it easier for people to plan a large-scale
biological attack. The authors found no statistically significant improvement
in plans produced with the assistance of AI versus withoug them.

The National Academies of Sciences, meanwhile,
[finds](https://www.nationalacademies.org/projects/DELS-BLS-24-04) that the
bottleneck to bioterrorism is not access to information. It's things like DNA
synthesis screening, tacit laboratory skill, culturing, formulation,
aerosolization -- all of which require human intervention, are expensive and
infamously prone to failure.

The government's own analysts, who have no consumer product to move and no
valuation to defend, have been telling us the answer for years in language so
measured that nobody has bothered to read it. AI merely increases the
magnitude and speed of threats we already have, ones that can be solved and
will exist regardless of AI.

Is hyperbole the only register we're able to communicate in?

It currently is, and none of this is going to change on the supply side.
Businesses are going to cast their products in the most favorable light. Media
is going to go with the headlines that draw attention.

I know, because I sometimes do it. When I published a piece last week
headlined "[Fuck 9/11](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/fuck-911)," I also
knew the headline would generate pearl-clutching outrage, and that the outrage
would carry the story a lot further than the argument would have on its own.

In a debate centered on whether a chatbot is going to become God, every major
faction is cashing in -- at the expense of us all.
